evidence.title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
evidence.effect: 63.9% reported reading labels was not too mentally demanding.
evidence.quote: They also reported that reading the labels was not too mentally demanding (no information overload; 63.9%).

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether designing AI device communications around information load, user familiarity, interaction frequency, and information placement improves user understanding. One vignette study of 340 patients found that 63.9% reported that reading AI labels was not too mentally demanding, which suggests the hazard may not affect most readers in that setting.

perspectives.view: No study compares communications designed with these four considerations against usual designs, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study used simulated vignettes in the United States with 340 patients. It measured perceived mental demand rather than comprehension, which limits its directness to the recommendation.

In the vignette study, 63.9% of patients reported that reading AI labels was not too mentally demanding. The study did not test whether patients understood key content or acted on it correctly. Perceived ease may not show whether important warnings are missed, so the safety effect of information placement and volume remains unmeasured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions states that additional information may detract from understanding, and FUTURE-AI calls for adjusting explanations for each end-user subgroup. Both are guidance documents using should language. The FDA text is a draft and does not create binding requirements, and neither source cites outcome data for this design approach.

The one hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and found that 63.9% did not find AI labels too mentally demanding. It did not report results for patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy, who may be the users most affected by dense or poorly placed information.

commentary.research_gap: Trials or usability studies are needed that compare AI device labels and interface text designed around information load, prior familiarity, interaction frequency, and placement against standard designs. These studies should measure comprehension and correct use in real clinical settings rather than self-reported mental demand in vignettes.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice. The single hazard study included a racial and ethnic minority focus but did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence does not show whether these groups experience information overload from AI device communications or whether design changes would help them.
